subChunks.title: What is a Test & the AAA Pattern
subChunks.hookHtml: A potion that hasn't been tested is not a potion — it's a gamble. Every formula in the Academy's lab is verified before it leaves the shelf. In software, we call that verification a test.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Why Write Tests?

A test is a piece of code that checks whether another piece of code works correctly. Benefits:

  • Confidence — you know the code works, not just hope it does
  • Regression prevention — if a future change breaks existing behaviour, a test catches it immediately
  • Documentation — tests show exactly how code is meant to be used
  • Design feedback — hard-to-test code is usually poorly designed; tests reveal coupling and missing abstraction

The AAA Pattern

Every test follows the same three-step structure:

  1. Arrange — set up inputs and the object under test
  2. Act — call the method you are testing
  3. Assert — check that the result matches what you expect
// Arrange
int a = 4;
int b = 6;
// Act
int result = add(a, b);
// Assert
if (result != 10) {
    System.out.println("FAIL: expected 10, got " + result);
} else {
    System.out.println("PASS");
}

What to Test

  • Happy path — typical valid input that produces the expected result
  • Edge cases — empty input, zero, negative, null, max value
  • Error cases — invalid input that should throw an exception

A Minimal Test Harness

Without JUnit (which you will learn in Sprint 2), you can write a simple assertEquals helper yourself:

public static void assertEquals(int expected, int actual, String label) {
    if (expected == actual) {
        System.out.println("PASS: " + label);
    } else {
        System.out.println("FAIL: " + label + " expected=" + expected + " actual=" + actual);
    }
}

This is essentially what JUnit's assertEquals does — it's not magic, just a comparison with a clear failure message.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's quality chamber is spotless — white marble floors, bright globes of light, and rows of identical test flasks. Every potion brewed downstairs is brought here before it goes anywhere else. A methodical wizard in a lab coat holds a clipboard.

storyBeats.speaker: Alchemist Proven
storyBeats.text: If you hand an untested spell to an adventurer and it misfires, who is responsible? You are. Testing is not optional. It is how professionals work. A test is simply code that checks whether other code behaves as intended.

storyBeats.speaker: Alchemist Proven
storyBeats.text: Every test follows the same pattern: Arrange — prepare the ingredients. Act — apply the formula. Assert — verify the result. Three steps. That's it. Arrange, Act, Assert — we call it the AAA pattern.

storyBeats.speaker: AAA test for a spell power calculator
Alchemist Proven
storyBeats.text: Test the happy path first — the normal case. Then the edge cases: what if level is 0? What if baseDamage is negative? What if both are 0? The edge cases are where bugs hide. A formula that works for '5 and 10' but explodes on '0 and 10' is not a tested formula.

Proven picks up a vial from the failed shelf. 'This one passed the happy path test. No one tested zero. A single adventurer used zero mana. The spell imploded.' She sets it back carefully. 'Write the edge cases first. Always.'

learningObjectives: Explain why automated tests are written and what benefits they provide
Structure a test using the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern
Write test cases for the happy path, edge cases, and error cases
Implement a simple assertEquals helper and use it to write verifiable tests
commonMistakes: Only testing the happy path and ignoring edge cases — most bugs live in edge cases
Testing multiple things in a single test — each test should verify exactly one behaviour
Writing tests after the code breaks, not before or alongside — tests written after the fact often unconsciously match the broken behaviour
Giving tests vague names — a test name should describe the input, the action, and the expected outcome
assessmentCriteria: Can write a test method following the AAA pattern with a clear label
Can identify the happy path, at least two edge cases, and one error case for a given method
Can implement a simple assertEquals method and use it to test an integer-returning method
Can explain what a regression is and how tests prevent them
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a software test is, why we write them, and what the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern means. Give a concrete example using a method you might test — like one that checks whether a number is even.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
You are given the method int clamp(int value, int min, int max) that constrains a value to the range [min, max]. Your task: write a test suite using the simple assertEquals helper already provided. Test:

  1. A value within range (should return unchanged)
  2. A value below min (should return min)
  3. A value above max (should return max)
  4. A value exactly equal to min (should return min)
  5. A value exactly equal to max (should return max)
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From scratch. Write a method boolean isPrime(int n) that returns true if n is a prime number, false otherwise. Also write an assertEquals-style helper: void assertBool(boolean expected, boolean actual, String label). Then write a test suite covering: n=2 (prime), n=1 (not prime), n=0 (not prime), n=7 (prime), n=9 (not prime), n=negative (not prime).

questions.questionHtml: In the AAA pattern, what does the Assert step do?
options: Sets up the inputs and objects needed for the test
Verifies that the actual result matches the expected result
Cleans up resources after the test
questions.correctAnswer: Verifies that the actual result matches the expected result
questions.explanationHtml: Assert is the verification step — it compares the actual output of the method under test against the expected value. If they differ, the test fails with a clear message. Without an assertion, you're not actually testing anything.

questions.questionHtml: You are writing tests for int abs(int n). Which set of test cases gives the best coverage?
questions.explanationHtml: Good test coverage includes: positive input (happy path), negative input (the main case the method handles), and zero (edge case). Testing three different positive values (option D) only tests one branch and ignores the critical negative-to-positive conversion.

questions.questionHtml: A test that checks only the happy path (typical valid input) provides complete test coverage.
questions.explanationHtml: The happy path only tests the normal case. Most bugs occur at edge cases (empty input, zero, null, boundaries) and error cases (invalid input). Complete coverage requires testing all three categories.

subChunks.title: Test Design & Introduction to JUnit
subChunks.hookHtml: Writing your own test harness shows you that testing is not magic. But professional Java projects use a standardised library called JUnit 5, which provides a richer vocabulary for expressing tests and integrates with every major tool in the ecosystem.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
JUnit 5 Basics

JUnit 5 is the standard Java testing framework. A JUnit test class contains methods annotated with @Test. JUnit discovers and runs them automatically:

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class SpellCalculatorTest {

    @Test
    void calcPower_level5_baseDamage10_returns50() {
        // Arrange
        int level = 5, base = 10;
        // Act
        int result = SpellCalculator.calcPower(level, base);
        // Assert
        assertEquals(50, result);
    }

    @Test
    void calcPower_levelZero_returnsZero() {
        assertEquals(0, SpellCalculator.calcPower(0, 10));
    }
}

Key JUnit Assertions

assertEquals(expected, actual)         // values are equal
assertNotEquals(unexpected, actual)    // values are not equal
assertTrue(condition)                  // condition is true
assertFalse(condition)                 // condition is false
assertNull(object)                     // object is null
assertNotNull(object)                  // object is not null
assertThrows(ExType.class, () -> ...)  // lambda throws expected exception

Naming Tests

Use descriptive method names: methodName_scenario_expectedResult(). When a test fails, the name tells you exactly what broke without opening the code:

// Good names:
void clamp_valueBelowMin_returnsMin()
void parse_nonNumericInput_throwsNumberFormatException()
void isEmpty_nullInput_returnsTrue()

// Bad name:
void test1()

assertThrows

To test that a method correctly throws an exception:

assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> {
    validateAge(-1);
});

This passes only if the lambda throws IllegalArgumentException. If it throws nothing (or a different exception), the test fails.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's quality assurance division has a shared testing ledger — a standard format that every alchemist, enchanter, and ward-keeper uses. No more hand-written notes on scraps of parchment. One format. One set of tools. Every test verifiable by anyone.

storyBeats.speaker: Quality Master Helios
storyBeats.text: JUnit 5 is Java's standard testing framework. You annotate a method with @Test and JUnit discovers and runs it for you. Every assertion you had to write manually — equals, true/false, null checks — JUnit provides out of the box.

storyBeats.speaker: A complete JUnit test class
Quality Master Helios
storyBeats.text: Name your tests precisely. The test name is the report. When 47 tests pass and one fails, the failure name must tell you exactly what broke: calcDamage_negativeLevel_throwsIllegalArgument. Not test3. Not myTest. The name is documentation.

Helios pulls out the ledger and runs a full suite. Green for each pass, red for one failure at the bottom. 'The test told us exactly what was wrong before anyone touched production,' he says. 'That is the whole point.'

learningObjectives: Recognise the @Test annotation and understand how JUnit discovers test methods
Use assertEquals, assertTrue, assertFalse, assertNull, and assertThrows correctly
Write descriptive test method names following the methodName_scenario_expectedResult convention
Understand that JUnit automates the test harness you built manually in the previous sub-chunk
commonMistakes: Reversing the expected and actual arguments in assertEquals — assertEquals(expected, actual) — always expected first
Using assertTrue(a.equals(b)) instead of assertEquals(a, b) — the latter gives a clearer failure message
Forgetting @Test — the method will not run
Putting multiple assertions for different scenarios in one test method — separate them so failures are isolated
assessmentCriteria: Can write a JUnit 5 test class with at least three @Test methods
Can use assertThrows to verify that a method throws the correct exception type
Can name test methods using the methodName_scenario_expectedResult convention
Can explain why assertEquals(expected, actual) order matters for error messages
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain JUnit 5 to someone who just learned to write their own test harness. What does JUnit add? How does it discover tests? What does assertThrows do that you couldn't easily do manually?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The method int divide(int a, int b) divides a by b and throws ArithmeticException if b is 0. Write a plain Java test class (no JUnit available in this sandbox) that tests:

  1. divide(10, 2) → 5
  2. divide(9, 3) → 3
  3. divide(0, 5) → 0
  4. divide(10, 0) → should throw ArithmeticException (catch it and print PASS if it does)

Use your own assertEquals(int expected, int actual, String label) helper. For the exception case, wrap in try-catch.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From scratch. Write a method String classify(int score) that returns: "Fail" for 0–49, "Pass" for 50–69, "Merit" for 70–84, "Distinction" for 85–100, and throws IllegalArgumentException for values outside 0–100. Write a full test suite covering: score=0, score=49, score=50, score=70, score=85, score=100, score=-1 (exception), score=101 (exception). Use your own helper for normal tests and try-catch for exception tests.

questions.questionHtml: In JUnit 5, methods annotated with @Test must be public.
questions.explanationHtml: JUnit 5 does not require test methods to be public. Package-private (default visibility) is fine and is actually the preferred style in modern JUnit 5 test classes.

questions.questionHtml: A test method is named test1() and checks that a list is not empty. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — test1 is a perfectly acceptable name
The name should describe the scenario and expected outcome, not just be a number
The method should be named testList()
Test methods cannot take no parameters
questions.correctAnswer: The name should describe the scenario and expected outcome, not just be a number
questions.explanationHtml: A good test name like addItem_nonEmptyList_containsItem() tells you what failed the moment a test report appears. test1 provides zero information — you must open the code to understand what it tests.

options: That validate(null) returns an IllegalArgumentException object
That validate(null) throws an IllegalArgumentException when executed
That validate(null) does not throw any exception
That null is an illegal argument
questions.correctAnswer: That validate(null) throws an IllegalArgumentException when executed
questions.explanationHtml: assertThrows executes the lambda and passes only if the specified exception type is thrown. If no exception is thrown, or a different exception type is thrown, the test fails.
